evidence: TS truncate() used s.length/s.slice() (UTF-16 units) while the Rust mirror used chars() (scalar values); for astral input the documented byte-identical contract genuinely diverges and TS could even slice a surrogate pair. Fix switches to code-point iteration via spread.
guidance_note: Write the astral/multi-codepoint boundary test alongside a byte-identical cross-runtime contract, not after review catches the divergence.

evidence: Verified against commit df64e2c: eslint-disable-next-line sits before 'case transient' and 'case permanent', which is where ESLint's no-fallthrough actually reports (the destination case) — the 'ok' case needs no suppression, so the specific claim that lint would fail is wrong. The broader point (duplicated process.exit(0) calls needing per-branch disables) was real and the planOutcome refactor removed it entirely.
guidance_note: Prefer a data-returning planner over a control-flow switch with per-branch side effects from the first pass, so no eslint-suppression residue accumulates for reviewers to flag.

evidence: The TS switch in interpretResponse had no default branch while the Rust mirror had one since kz8.4; an unrecognized wire code fell through and returned undefined, propagating an impossible ClientOutcome. This switch was part of the original df64e2c commit, not caused by any fix in this batch.
guidance_note: When porting a switch that has a defensive default in one runtime, port the default branch in the same commit as the rest of the switch.

evidence: alive was scoped per loop-iteration and the post-loop guard checked socket-file existence, a proxy that can be true while accept() never armed; lifting alive to loop scope makes readiness measure the actual dependency.
guidance_note: Test readiness on the property the test depends on (accept() succeeding), not a cheaper proxy (file existing) that can be true while the property is false.

evidence: sendShutdown() had no per-call timeout, so a hung daemon degraded the failure signal to jest's generic 30s timeout instead of naming the call that hung. Fix adds a deadline timer sharing SHUTDOWN_BUDGET_MS.
guidance_note: Every async test helper needs its own deadline, or a hang surfaces as the harness's generic timeout instead of pointing at the call that stalled.

evidence: The incident doc hard-coded server.ts:NNN references that this very PR's fixes immediately obsoleted; reframed as a point-in-time artifact and ~30 line-number suffixes stripped.
guidance_note: Write incident/audit docs with file+concept anchors, not line numbers, since the fix the doc motivates will itself move those lines.

evidence: RENDER_FAILED is an internal processing failure, not a semantic refusal, so the comment's two-way taxonomy was inaccurate; reworded to name the real invariant (recovery class) that covers both refusals and internal failures.

Embedded newlines in a daemon error string would violate the documented one-line glyph contract; the existing corpus never contained newlines so the gap was invisible to tests. This gap predates every fix in this thread — it is present in the original error_glyph.rs from its creation and untouched by F1's own code-point fix — the ON-POST-REVIEW-COMMIT flag here is an artifact of b1935d7 (a docs-only commit) being HEAD at round 7, not evidence the gap was introduced by a fix in this batch.
guidance_note: The 'single line' contract needs a fixture with an embedded newline, not just a shape assertion that happens to never see one.

evidence: Same newline-sanitization gap as F8, on the TS mirror. Present since the original error-glyph.ts implementation, not caused by any earlier fix in this thread; b1935d7 is coincidentally HEAD at this round.

MismatchServer.port actually held a Unix socket path passed to net.createConnection({path}), never a TCP port; renamed to sockPath across the interface. Unrelated to b1935d7 (a docs commit) — this test file predates that commit.

planOutcome() and its 'Pure mapping' header comment were both introduced by F2's fix (commit c356cda); the same commit that added the purity claim also added the debug() side effect, so the fix's own comment overstated the property its own code shipped with.
guidance_note: When a refactor's comment asserts a property (purity) as the selling point of the change, write a test that would fail if the same commit's implementation violates it.

evidence: resp comes from an unchecked 'frame as Response' cast; if a daemon/stub omits a string error, undefined would propagate into ClientOutcome.message and crash truncate()'s code-point iteration. This switch/cast predates F11's fix (unrelated file, outcome-plan.ts vs client.ts).
guidance_note: Every field read off an unchecked wire-JSON cast needs its own narrowing, not just the fields exercised by the happy-path tests.

evidence: daemonV: resp.daemonV ?? 0 trusted the cast's runtime type; a non-number daemonV would carry through to the visible glyph. Same trust-boundary class as F12, same fix commit (c323be3), unrelated to F11's outcome-plan.ts fix that happens to be round14's other content.

interpretException funneled every sendOne() failure (including JSON-parse and oversized-frame errors) through the transient path, which would kick the daemon on garbage frames and reintroduce the exact respawn spiral this PR fixes. This catch-all was part of the original client.ts content (visible in the F14 diff hunk as pre-existing code), not caused by any earlier finding.
guidance_note: When a catch block widens to 'anything that throws is transient', enumerate the actual failure classes (protocol violation vs. IO/connect error) before shipping, since a parse failure and a dead socket need opposite recovery actions.

evidence: classify_io_error routed InvalidData/InvalidInput (oversized-frame protocol violations) to transient, symmetric with the TS-side F14 bug and same root cause (pre-existing, paired fix in c323be3).
The elapsed-time assertion duplicated the Promise.race timer's own enforcement and was flaky on ms-granularity plus post-exit scheduling overhead; removed as redundant with the race's rejection.

Rust unit tests hard-coded client_v/daemon_v, so they would silently stop testing the real contract (or need editing) on every PROTOCOL_VERSION bump; derived fixtures from the canonical constant instead. Test content predates this round, independent of F16's daemon-shutdown.test.ts fix.
guidance_note: Version-numbered test fixtures should derive from the canonical constant at the point they're first written, not hard-code the current value.

evidence: Same hard-coded-version issue as F17, on the TS mirror; fixed symmetrically by deriving CLIENT_V/OTHER_V from PROTOCOL_VERSION.

asNumber(), introduced by F13's fix (c323be3) to narrow resp.daemonV, accepted any finite number; Rust's as_u64() falls back to 0 for negatives/fractionals, so the same wire payload (daemonV: -1 or 3.14) would diverge across runtimes. F13's fix closed the wrong-type gap but not the wrong-range gap in the same helper.
guidance_note: When adding a trust-boundary narrowing helper, enumerate the full domain of the cross-runtime contract (type AND range/integrality), not just the type check that fixes the reported case.

evidence: truncate() (Rust) sanitized \n/\r per F8's fix (a6cc150) but still passed through ESC and other C0 controls; since BAD_REQUEST messages echo caller-supplied values (e.g. an unknown click verb), a crafted string could inject terminal escapes. F8's newline-only predicate was the incomplete instance of the broader 'sanitize the glyph body' requirement.
guidance_note: A sanitize-boundary fix for one hazard class (line-breaking chars) should ask what OTHER control characters break the same invariant (terminal styling) before shipping, not just the one the reviewer named.

evidence: Same gap as F20 on the TS mirror (F9's fix). This is a real ANSI-injection vector, not a style nit: a crafted daemon message could truncate the styled envelope with \x1b[0m.

The throw-on-failure branch that F4's fix (767ca85) added to spawnDaemon() kills the child but never runs the rmSync cleanup for stateRoot/XDG_CACHE_HOME/XDG_CONFIG_HOME that the success path's handle.cleanup() already had — F4 fixed the readiness signal but left the new failure branch without the cleanup wiring the success branch already had.
guidance_note: When adding a new throw/failure branch alongside an existing success-path cleanup, route both through one cleanup primitive in the same commit — don't let the new branch skip resource teardown the old branch already does.

evidence: A JS timer cannot fire during a truly synchronous thread block (no event-loop tick, no callback), so 'bounds a synchronous hang inside close()' overstated what the non-unref'd SIGKILL timer can do. This backstop-first restructuring was part of the original PR submission (commit e92259a, before round 0), not caused by any finding in this batch. Comment now correctly scopes the guarantee to async-handle retention, matching the documented 452-corpse failure mode.

Verified against a276bb1 and docs/process-spawning-audit.md: the documented incident was that process.exit(0) reached the call site but did not terminate the process (daemons stayed alive 42 minutes, holding the socket fd) — an anomaly, not normal Node semantics. The non-unref'd SIGKILL timer is a deliberate backstop for exactly that anomalous path; in the normal path it correctly does nothing because exit() already terminated. The reviewer's suggested exitCode+return shape doesn't fix a real defect, just expresses different (undesired) intent — allowing continued execution the daemon's lifecycle doesn't have. The shutdown contract test already pins the required behavior. No code changed after this finding, consistent with the pushback being upheld.

F21's C0+DEL sanitize predicate (82472cf) missed the C1 range, notably U+009B (8-bit CSI), which some terminals interpret as an escape introducer — a live ANSI-injection bypass even without literal \x1b. Widened to the full Unicode Cc category on both runtimes.
guidance_note: When closing a terminal-injection vector, sanitize against the full control-character category (Unicode Cc / C0+C1+DEL), not just the ASCII subset the first reported payload used.

evidence: interpretException, introduced by F14's fix (c323be3) to route protocol violations to permanent/malformed_response, did so via brittle substring matching on error messages ('Unexpected token' etc.) — functionally correct for the cases tested but fragile across Node versions/locales, and a [LAW:types-are-the-program] violation in the same sense F14 was fixing. Replaced with a ProtocolError type thrown at the source.
guidance_note: When a fix routes behavior off a caught exception's message text, that's provisional — follow up in the same change by giving the throw site a typed error so the classification isn't string-matching.

narrative: A 26-finding, 30-round marathon fixing a real production incident (daemon respawn spiral) with paired TS/Rust mirrors; almost every finding was a genuine, correctly-accepted catch, and the two pushbacks (F2's partial dispute, F24's full pushback) both held up under verification against the actual diffs and the incident doc. The real cost was six small chains where a fix's own scope was too narrow: a 'pure' comment shipped with a side effect (F2->F11), a new readiness fix's failure branch skipped cleanup the success branch had (F4->F22), and three separate trust/sanitization boundaries (daemonV range, control-char sanitization x2) got fixed for the reported instance but not the full domain, each requiring a follow-up round (F8->F20, F9->F21->F25, F13->F19, F14->F26).
guidance_observations: Every 'sanitize/narrow at this boundary' fix in this PR needed a second pass because the first pass matched the reported payload rather than the full hazard class (all control chars, all invalid ranges, all failure kinds) — enumerate the domain once instead of iterating finding-by-finding.

The agent's pushbacks were well-grounded in the PR's own incident documentation (docs/process-spawning-audit.md) rather than assertion, and held up on independent verification — citing the concrete prior incident evidence is what made them credible, not the law tokens attached to them.
A 'pure function' or 'single enforcer' comment written in the same commit as the code should be checked against that code before the commit lands, not left for a reviewer to catch the mismatch (F11).

evidence: The cache key used the raw $TMUX value (socket,pid,session) instead of just the socket path, so two clients on the same tmux server would miss the cache; fixed to key on the substring before the first comma, with a test proving two client-pid suffixes share one entry.

recordStart runs before the spawn attempt and arms the limiter on a failed spawn too (a test already pins this), so the comment's 'successful spawn-starts' wording was inaccurate; reworded to describe attempts and explain why arming-by-attempt is intentional (stops a broken binary from being retried in a tight loop).

The new test added by F1's fix (7930c41) used withEnv({TMUX_PANE}) but mutated process.env.TMUX directly inside the test body without including it in withEnv, leaking TMUX into later tests. The leak is in test code F1's own fix introduced, not a pre-existing gap.
guidance_note: A test helper like withEnv should snapshot/restore every env var the test body mutates, not just the ones passed in — or the helper itself should assert no other env keys changed.

evidence: Same TMUX env-leak pattern as F3, in the sibling test also added by F1's fix (7930c41).

New TTL-floor tests hard-coded 500 instead of importing MIN_SHELL_TTL_MS, which would silently stop testing the real floor if it changes; exported the constant and bound the test sleep to it. This is original feature-test content, not caused by an earlier finding in this batch.

Reviewer wanted fake timers to cut the ~700ms real-wait tests; the agent correctly explains fake timers can't advance real subprocess execution (the OS schedules /bin/cat, not the Jest runner) so switching would make the tests wrong, not just faster — a valid technical rebuttal to the literal suggestion. But the agent still changed the sleep duration/derivation (binding it to MIN_SHELL_TTL_MS + TTL_TICK_BUFFER_MS) in response, which is a real (if partial) accommodation of the reviewer's underlying complaint about magic numbers, not a pure hold-the-line pushback.
guidance_note: When a reviewer's suggested mechanism (fake timers) can't work for a stated reason (real subprocess I/O), say so explicitly as the plan before implementing a different concession, so the thread doesn't read as a straight accept when it was actually a rebuttal-plus-partial-fix.

evidence: The header comment said null meant only 'reported no session', but the code also caches null on any spawn error/timeout (!result.ok); updated the comment to state both null-producing paths. This is a comment-accuracy fix on the original implementation, not caused by an earlier finding.

narrative: A small, clean PR (rate-limiting, TTL floor, tmux cache) where every finding was accepted and every fix was correct; round 1's five findings included two (F3, F4) that were self-inflicted — the new tests F1's own fix added to prove the cache-key change leaked the TMUX env var into later tests. No round was fully avoidable since round 1 also carried three independent, valid findings on other files.
guidance_observations: A fix that adds new tests using withEnv-style env-mutation helpers should audit the same commit for env vars mutated but not passed to the helper, since that's exactly the kind of self-inflicted finding a reviewer catches next round.

evidence: The new comment claimed launch/launchSync are always 'waited' with the child 'reaped before the caller resumes', but the async timeout path resolved on the timer itself without waiting for the close event, so a timed-out child could outlive the caller frame — contradicting the stated invariant. Agent chose to fix the code (wait for close, SIGTERM then SIGKILL after grace) rather than weaken the comment, which is the correct call since the invariant is the PR's whole point.
The guard test excluded files by basename == 'launch.rs', bypassable by a future src/foo/launch.rs; tightened to compare the exact path.
The new cargo test job had no Rust toolchain setup step, unlike build-rust; added the same dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable step so the guard doesn't rely on ambient runner tooling.

Verified against commit 4eee1a8 (the original round-0 commit): the substring-only match on 'Command::new(' was present at test creation, before F2's fix (68e82bd) ever touched this test — F2's fix only changed the file-exemption check (basename to exact path), not the detection predicate. The ON-NAMED-FIX-COMMIT flag on 68e82bd is a false positive: this aliasing gap (use ... as Cmd; Cmd::new()) is a pre-existing weakness in the original guard, first surfaced in round 1, not a consequence of F2's fix.
guidance_note: When writing a source-scan guard against a construct, enumerate every syntactic way to reach that construct (direct call, qualified path, import-and-alias) before shipping the first version, not after a reviewer finds the aliasing bypass.

evidence: Verified against commit 68e82bd (F1's fix): it replaced 'if (!settled) child.kill("SIGTERM")' with an unconditional 'child.kill("SIGTERM")' plus a new unconditional SIGKILL escalation, dropping even the settled guard the old code had. Agent reproduced the crash: killing a pid-less child (async ENOENT spawn error) terminated the *caller* process. F1's rewrite of the timeout-escalation path introduced (or at minimum removed the partial protection against, and added a second unconditional kill call exposed to) this crash; gated both kill calls on child.pid !== undefined.
guidance_note: When rewriting a kill/signal path to drop an existing settled-style guard, check what invariant that guard was actually protecting (here, partially: a pid-less child) before removing it, and replace it with the correct guard rather than none.

evidence: Verified against commit e77619f (F4's fix): it added 'body.contains("process::Command")' as a new detection branch to close the aliasing gap. That exact substring is a prefix of unrelated identifiers like std::os::unix::process::CommandExt, so F4's own new check would false-positive on legitimate code (e.g. CommandExt) that built fine before F4's fix landed — a real regression in guard reliability introduced by the fix meant to tighten it. Tightened to require a non-identifier character after the match.
guidance_note: When widening a substring-based guard to catch an aliasing bypass, check the new substring isn't a prefix of an unrelated, legitimate identifier before shipping it.

evidence: Verified against commit 68e82bd (F1's fix): it added the new SIGTERM-ignoring test using '/bin/sh -c "trap '' TERM; sleep 5"' to prove the SIGKILL escalation. When the parent shell is SIGKILL'ed, the sleep grandchild can survive as an orphan for seconds — a leak in the new test itself (an 'ironic leak in a no-leak PR'), not a defect in the production escalation logic F1 shipped. Switched to a single SIGTERM-ignoring node process with no child to orphan.
guidance_note: A test that proves a 'no orphaned process' guarantee should itself be checked for orphaning risk (e.g. a shell wrapping a grandchild) before it's added, since it's exactly the failure mode under test.

narrative: A tight, four-round PR closing the process-lifetime guarantee; round 0's three findings were all genuine and correctly fixed. But round 1's finding (F4) was a pre-existing gap in the original guard, not caused by anything in this batch, while round 2's entire slate (F5, F6, F7) was self-inflicted: F1's timeout-escalation rewrite dropped its own kill-guard and shipped a test that leaks an orphan shell child, and F4's own aliasing fix introduced a new false-positive substring match. Round 2 would not have existed had F1 and F4's fixes been complete on the first pass.
guidance_observations: Every finding in round 2 was a bug in code the immediately preceding round's fix had just written — verify a fix against the same failure classes (crash-on-edge-input, false-positive-on-legitimate-input, resource-leak-in-new-test) the original finding was about before pushing, since one round of review is being spent per self-inflicted defect.
